query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy nanoalloys used for high‐temperature applications, the overall structural and chemical stability is governed by a competition between the configurational entropy (which tends to stabilize a disordered solid solution) and the enthalpic contributions from specific elemental pair interactions (e.g., a strong attractive interaction between Al and Ni) that promote short‐range ordering or clustering. At elevated temperatures, while the high mixing entropy favors a homogeneous phase, residual chemical affinities induce localized ordering that sets the limits of stability.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanoalloy in a near-equiatomic high-entropy solid solution state (e.g., Al0.1CrCoFeNi) synthesized by methods such as gas-atomization to ensure fine, uniformly mixed particles.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of nanoalloys: one with a known strongly interacting elemental pair (e.g., including a small addition of Al to drive Al-Ni chemical affinity) and a variant lacking that component or with a reduced concentration. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature annealing treatments.
generation.conditions: Annealing in an inert atmosphere at a temperature just below the melting point (e.g., 0.8 Tm) for a controlled duration (e.g., several hours) with in situ monitoring by high-temperature X-ray diffraction (XRD) and complementary real-space characterization via high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM).
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical short-range order (SRO) manifested as atomic clustering or ordering domains driven by specific pair correlations (e.g., Al-Al and Ni-Ni versus Al-Ni ordering) that emerge in the nanoalloy.
generation.mechanism: The mechanism involves the intrinsic driving force from favorable pairwise enthalpic interactions—which tend to reduce the free energy by forming chemically ordered clusters—competing with the entropy-driven tendency towards random mixing. Under high-temperature conditions, while the configurational entropy largely dominates to maintain a single-phase solid solution, the residual attractive interactions can locally overcome entropy, leading to detectable SRO that governs the structural/chemical stability boundaries.
generation.predicted_outcome: In the alloy variant containing the strongly interacting pair, one would observe a measurable increase in short-range ordering or clustering (evidenced by split or shifted diffraction peaks and local compositional fluctuations in HRTEM) relative to the baseline that lacks that pair. This increased ordering should be more pronounced upon modest cooling from high temperature but remains stable at high temperature, while the baseline nanoalloy maintains a more uniform distribution.
generation.baseline: The high-entropy nanoalloy lacking a strong affinity pair (or with reduced concentration), which primarily displays random atomic distributions stabilized solely by the high configurational entropy.
generation.boundary: This prediction holds for high temperatures (approaching but below the melting range, e.g., ~0.8 Tm) and is valid for nanoalloys where surface and size effects do not dominate the ordering process. It may not apply if the annealing times or temperatures are so high as to activate significant diffusion resulting in complete phase separation or if kinetic effects overshadow the thermodynamic driving forces.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative magnitude of the ordering may depend on the specific alloy system, processing history, and nanoscale constraints; furthermore, kinetic factors during heating and cooling may partially mask the equilibrium ordering tendencies.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct in situ high-temperature XRD and HRTEM observations on both the modified (with strong Al-Ni interactions) and control nanoalloy samples during and after annealing at ~0.8 Tm. Quantify the degree of short-range order via peak splitting/shifts and by mapping local compositional variations. In addition, perform differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to detect ordering transitions.
measurements: XRD peak profiles as a function of temperature/time
HRTEM imaging to identify nanoclusters or compositional modulations
DSC curves showing exothermic/endothermic events tied to ordering transitions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the modified and control nanoalloys exhibit statistically equivalent degrees of chemical homogeneity (i.e., no significant differences in SRO features, diffraction peak profiles, or DSC signals) under identical high-temperature processing, then the hypothesis that specific elemental pair interactions govern the stability will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study AlxCrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. In this report, we establish a force-field for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy and validate it by comparing structural properties, relative stability, and pair probabilities with first-principles calculations and limited experimental results. After the validation, we employ the new potential to investigate the large-scale deformation characteristics of Al0.1CrCoFeNi using atomistic MD simulations. Thus, we address the absence of well-developed force-field functions for high-entropy alloys and provide the EAM-LJ parameters to define the self- and cross-interactions of the participating elements in the alloy. In Al0.1CrCoFeNi, the electronic-structure-based linear-response calculations predict clustering driven by Al-Ni pair correlations (forcing Al-Al and Ni-Ni clustering behavior). The MD simulations are in agreement with the clustering trend, as given by the large clustering domains of like pairs dominated by Al-Al. Although an increase in temperature reduces the clustering strength of like pairs, Al-Al correlations still dominate. cited_evidence.text: Figure 2IIa shows the B2-BCC structural energy difference calculated from the RBA model plotted together with the FCC-BCC difference as a function of n. It is found from the RBA calculations that competition between the FCC and B2 phases starts at valence electron concentration, n ≈ 8. Comparison with the present experimental data for CCFN-Al0.5 (n = 7.67) where FCC peaks are indicated in XRD (Fig. IIc), shows that the RBA model may overestimate the stability of the B2 phase. However, in comparison with a new HEA composition, AlCoCrFeNi2.1, where the corresponding valence electron concentration is n = 7.70, the experimental observation of an FCC/B2 dual-phase constitution. Furthermore, experimental evidence of B2 presence has also been reported in CCFN-Al0.75, CCFN-Al1, and CCFN-Al1.5 with n values ranging from 6.57 to 7.41. These observations not only validate our theoretical prediction but also demonstrate that the formation of B2 phase is strongly correlated with the short-range chemical order between Al and the excess composition of Ni transition metals in the HEAs, suggesting possible effects of the processing method and cooling rate, as noted by Dahlborg et al..
